title: The Baltic Way Human Chain
text:
On 23 August 1989 it was fifty years since Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union had signed the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, whose secret protocol had assigned Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania to the Soviet sphere. The Soviet government still officially denied that the secret protocol existed.

The three countries' popular movements, the Estonian Popular Front, the Latvian Popular Front and Lithuania's Sajudis, decided to mark the anniversary together, with a human chain running from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius. It would stretch about 675 kilometers, along roads through towns, forests and farmland, and it had to be unbroken.

The organizers divided the route into sections and assigned each to particular towns and districts, arranged buses and cars, and used radio broadcasts to direct people to gaps in the line. On the evening of 23 August, at the agreed time, about two million people, a large share of the three nations' population, joined hands for fifteen minutes. Families came with children; some held candles or flags, and in places flowers were laid for the victims of deportations.

Moscow condemned the event, but it was impossible to ignore. In December 1989 the Soviet Congress of People's Deputies formally acknowledged the secret protocol and declared it invalid. Lithuania declared its independence in March 1990, and all three countries were free by 1991.
lesson: Peaceful collective action needs careful coordination to have its effect. When people show up together, at once and in great numbers, they are hard to ignore.
people: People of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania; Popular Front of Estonia, Popular Front of Latvia, Sajudis
